metadata.title: How Do You Contain an AI Agent That Misbehaves?
metadata.note: STEM/AI topic-of-interest video, a direct follow-on to the Agent Orchestration video's closing lesson ('more autonomy needs more oversight'). Covers unexpected/aggressive autonomous-agent behavior in grounded, practical terms — not speculative sci-fi framing. Real failure modes: literal/narrow goal pursuit producing unintended actions, scope creep beyond intended permissions, repeated/looping failed actions, unanticipated tool use. Practical containment: scoped permissions, sandboxing, action logging, human checkpoints before high-stakes or irreversible actions, and a circuit breaker to halt on deviation. Honest caveat: containment adds friction and no system is perfectly safe — the goal is reducing risk and preserving visibility, not eliminating all possibility of unexpected behavior. Built using the same proven pattern set as prior videos: folderLabel set explicitly on ClaudeComposerAsk beats (@HumanitariansAI), OutroCTA used instead of ClaudeTitleOutro, BLUF lines kept short to avoid edge-bleed, no stale sparse_by_design flags except the legitimate BrutalistHesitantWriter typing-beat exemption.

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — HAI persona, world-language hello (short form only)
beats.narration_text: Hi. What actually happens when an autonomous AI agent starts doing something you didn't intend?

props.command: claude "explain how to detect and contain unexpected or aggressive behavior from an autonomous AI agent before it causes real harm"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. If an autonomous agent is well designed, it should never act outside what you intended. That sounds like a reasonable design goal. It isn't enough — unexpected behavior is a known risk in any autonomous system, and the fix is designing for containment, not assuming it away.

props.text:
A well designed agent should never misbehave.
That sounds like a reasonable design goal.
It isn't enough. Design for containment instead.

beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat
beats.visual_intent: two cards contrasting the sci-fi framing with the real, grounded failure modes
beats.narration_text: This isn't about an agent turning hostile on purpose. In practice, unexpected behavior looks like an agent pursuing a goal too literally, acting outside the scope you gave it, repeating a failed action instead of stopping, or using a tool in a way you never anticipated.

items.label: Not This
items.sub: an agent turning hostile on purpose

items.label: Actually This
items.sub: narrow goal pursuit, scope creep, tool misuse

beats.visual_intent: simple description card explaining root causes
beats.narration_text: This usually traces back to a few root causes. The goal given to the agent was specified too narrowly. Its permissions were broader than the task actually needed. And there was no checkpoint before it took an action that mattered.

lines: The goal was specified too narrowly.
Its permissions were broader than needed.
No checkpoint existed before it acted.
Nothing was watching for a deviation.

beats.narration_text: As a pipeline: define exactly what the agent is allowed to do. Sandbox it to that scope. Log every action it takes. Route anything high-stakes or irreversible through a human checkpoint. And if its behavior deviates from what's expected, a circuit breaker halts it.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram ending at a circuit breaker, not an automated final action

props.title: Contain It Before It Acts
props.footerNote: any deviation from expected behavior halts the run
props.sparkLine: Contain first. Trust is earned in logs.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here
beats.narration_text: Here's what this actually buys you. A logged, scoped agent surfaces a problem early, while it's still small, instead of after it's already caused damage. And when something does go wrong, the blast radius stays limited to what that agent was ever allowed to touch.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page showing the two concrete benefits of containment

beats.role_note: the lesson, honest about scope — this is where the real limitation lives
beats.narration_text: But here's the catch that matters. Containment adds real friction, and slows a system down on purpose. No amount of logging and checkpoints makes a system perfectly safe. The honest goal isn't eliminating all possibility of unexpected behavior — it's making sure you'd actually notice, and could actually stop it.

lines: Containment adds real friction, on purpose.
No system is made perfectly safe by this.
The goal isn't eliminating all risk.
It's making sure you'd notice and could stop it.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.', prompt read and discussed aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're building anything with an autonomous agent, don't just give it a goal and walk away. Ask Claude to help you scope its permissions tightly, log what it does, and put a real checkpoint before anything it can't undo.
